expected.text: Goudin and Sperling define motion as the act of a being in potency insofar as it is in potency; Rohault and Le Grand define it as a body's transfer from the neighbourhood of the bodies touching it, and call the scholastic definition obscure
Rohault and Le Grand make God the first and general cause of motion, conserving the same quantity of motion in the world
Goudin and Sperling hold that whatever is moved is moved by another (omne quod movetur ab alio movetur) and divide motion into natural and violent
Goudin treats the kinds of motion as the four of Aristotle (generation, alteration, augmentation, local motion) or the three of motion proper
Rohault treats reflection and refraction mechanically, as a ball striking a surface or passing between media, with equal angles of incidence and reflection
Le Grand's V a. 6 derives refraction as Descartes did in the Dioptrique (the tennis ball), with sines in constant ratio
Sperling and Goudin have no reflection or refraction in their motion sections
Rohault departs from Descartes on at least one rule of impact, appealing to experiment
Sperling names Galileo or Scaliger on motion
The topic needs new questions: what motion is; whether whatever is moved is moved by another; natural and violent motion; the equality of the angles of reflection; the cause of refraction
